counted_texts.text: Sambalpur district’s cultural account uses Sambalpuri for speech in western Odisha. It places language alongside singing, dancing and seasonal gatherings.

The district account describes Dalkhai through group song and dance. Its account of Nuakhai follows new paddy from offerings to the sharing of new rice by the eldest family member, then greetings. These are specific ways of bringing people together; the description cannot stand for every household’s practice.

A recording, a radio play and a family gathering ask different things of a voice. Following those settings gives a fuller starting point than treating one celebrated song as the whole language. Ask which version, writer or local name matters to the person speaking.
The 2022 interview with lyricist Mitrabhanu Gountia also uses “Sambalpuri-Kosali”. That is the interview’s wording, not proof that every speaker uses both names interchangeably.
“Rangabati” brings four makers together: Mitrabhanu Gountia wrote the lyrics, Prabhudatta Pradhan composed the music, and Jitendriya Haripal and Krishna Patel sang it.

In the interview, Gountia recalls a radio sequence with a female solo, a male solo and then the duet. The commercial recording retained only the duet. This is his recollection of the versions, not an independently checked recording chronology.
He recalls publishing the essay “Pariksha Chinta” in his school magazine, Prabaha, before radio invitations led him towards lyrics, radio plays and musical features in Sambalpuri.
Odisha Review · Interview with Mitrabhanu Gountia (January 2022)
